extracted.intended_audience: students of philosophy and literary theory; poets, critics, and readers concerned with aesthetics and moral effects of art
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and normative claims about imitation (poetry, painting) — what makes an art truthful, useful, or harmful — and how arts affect the soul and the polis. Useful for evaluating or producing poetry with regard to truth, moral effect, and social usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold taxonomy of arts (use, make, imitate)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three arts which are concerned with all things: one which uses, another which makes, a third which imitates them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes the roles and epistemic standing of users, makers, and imitators. Example: the flute-player (user) knows best which flutes are satisfactory and instructs the flute-maker, who thereby attains correct belief; the imitator (painter/poet) neither knows from use nor attains true opinion merely by copying. This taxonomy grounds later claims about relative truth and authority among arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence is relative to intended use
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence or beauty or truth of every structure, animate or inanimate, and of every action of man, is relative to the use for which nature or the artist has intended them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional standard: an object's or work's goodness is judged by fitness for its intended purpose. Practitioners (users) who employ the object in context have privileged knowledge to judge and instruct makers; makers’ judgments derive from users' reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Users (practitioners) are epistemic authorities for craft
rubrics_metrics.description: The user of instruments must have the greatest experience of them, and he must indicate to the maker the good or bad qualities which develop themselves in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical crafts should be informed by those who use the work in real contexts (e.g., a flute-player advising a flute-maker). Makers who ignore user-experience risk producing inferior artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is thrice removed from truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is concerned with that which is thrice removed from the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitative artists (painters, poets) represent appearances rather than reality or the craftsman’s functional forms; they produce representations of representations and thus cannot reach truth or knowledge. This is supported by analogy to visual illusions and conjuring which exploit sensory weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative art yields opinion, not knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The instrument (or depiction) is the same, but about the excellence or badness of it the maker will only attain to a correct belief; the imitator will no more have true opinion than he will have knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whereas users and makers can have knowledge or correct belief anchored in function and practice, imitators only form opinions shaped by appearances and social imitation; therefore their claims about 'goodness' lack epistemic grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative arts address inferior parts of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting or drawing, and imitation in general, are far removed from truth, and the companions and friends and associates of a principle within us which is equally removed from reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation appeals to and strengthens irrational, emotional parts of the soul (grief, laughter, lust, anger) rather than the rational/calculating principle; hence it cultivates dispositions that are 'inferior' and may corrupt judgment and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular poetry panders to passions, not reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative poet who aims at being popular is not by nature made, nor is his art intended, to please or to affect the rational principle in the soul; but he will prefer the passionate and fitful temper, which is easily imitated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets seeking popular appeal will depict extreme passions or volatile characters because these are easy for crowds to imitate; this is an anti-pattern if the goal is to educate reasoned character or civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry can harm by training emotions and lowering restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry feeds and waters the passions instead of drying them up; she lets them rule, although they ought to be controlled, if mankind are ever to increase in happiness and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sympathetic responses to tragic recitations may make one less able to moderate personal sorrow; comic jests heard publicly may free one from shame and encourage indecorous speech at home. Thus poetic effect on affective habits is a key criterion: does it strengthen restraint and reason or the reverse?

rubrics_metrics.name: Calm, virtuous characters are difficult to represent and appreciate
rubrics_metrics.description: The wise and calm temperament, being always nearly equable, is not easy to imitate or to appreciate when imitated, especially at a public festival when a promiscuous crowd is assembled in a theatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art that aims to cultivate virtue cannot rely on immediate dramatic spectacle; its subjects (temperate, rational characters) are less spectacular and thus less likely to satisfy popular tastes, though they are more aligned with moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible poetry must serve moral and civic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Hymns to the gods and praises of famous men are the only poetry which ought to be admitted into our State. If there is a use in poetry as well as a delight, it may be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State (or community) should admit only those poetic forms that demonstrably support law, reason, and virtue. Poets must prove usefulness — defenders may speak in verse or prose to show poetry's benefit to human life and the polis; mere pleasantness is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic defense requirement (usefulness test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let her (poetry) make a defence of herself in lyrical or some other metre... let them show not only that she is pleasant but also useful to States and to human life, and we will listen in a kindly spirit; for if this can be proved we shall surely be the gainers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural standard: allow poetry to be reinstated only after a demonstrated defense of its utility. This functions as an evaluative test for creative work: can it be shown to promote civic/moral goods, not merely entertain?

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware imitation as mere play/illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is only a kind of play or sport, and the tragic poets ... are imitators in the highest degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat works that operate primarily as spectacle or illusion skeptically when assessing their truth-producing or educational capacity. Imitation as 'play' lacks the seriousness required for moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational calculation rescues us from sensory deception
rubrics_metrics.description: The arts of measuring and numbering and weighing come to the rescue of the human understanding—there is the beauty of them—and the apparent greater or less, or more or heavier, no longer have the mastery over us, but give way before calculation and measure and weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value forms of art and discourse that appeal to reason, measure, and calculation to correct sensory illusions. In literary terms, privileging rational clarity and proportion over deceptive appearances is a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should not encourage contradiction within the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation imitates actions of men ... and the soul has been acknowledged by us to be full of these and ten thousand similar oppositions occurring at the same moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess creative works for whether they promote inner conflict and instability (by reinforcing irrational impulses) or whether they help harmonize the soul's parts. Favor works that foster unity of soul through reasoned moral formation.
